Transcript body:
[00:00] Lena: all right everyone good afternoon thanks for joining today's weekly poc sync. this is lena from redwood, with marco on the call and ruth at the end for cs support. quick agenda: results review, tuning items, next steps.
[00:22] Jared: yep thanks lena, we've got priya, dana, and tom on. we ran the extended job last night, should have numbers, the costs were a bit higher than expected so want to dig into that.
[00:38] Marco: cool, i'll start with a quick recap of the bench. we ran your typical chat workload with the 2.7B open model variant pinned — note we used 8k context and 1k response avg. baseline (no prefix caching) gave us about 18k tokens/min on one g4-like instance, which maps to roughly 300 tokens/sec. cost baseline measured at about $11 per 100k tokens using the hosted configuration we ran against.
[01:10] Priya: sorry can you repeat the $ per 100k? i thought the number last week was closer to $7.
[01:18] Marco: yeah last week we used more aggressive batching. this run was a conservative default (batch size ~8, timeout 40ms) and no kv caching; that moves more tokens to be realtime and reduces batching efficiency, so cost went up. for clarity: this run showed approx $11/100k, but with batching tuned to 32 and prefix cache on we simulated down to $4.9/100k in our model.
[01:48] Dana: that's a big swing. how reliable is that simulated $4.9?
[01:52] Marco: it's a projection based on measured hit-rates and batching improvements. the key levers are cache hit-rate and effective batch size. in our simulation if prefix cache hit-rate is 60% and batch size goes to 24 effective, tokens/sec jumps ~2.8x and cost per token drops ~55%.
[02:20] Tom: what's the prefix cache again? is that the kv cache we talked about?
[02:24] Lena: yes sometimes called kv cache or prefix caching — stores recent prefixes per session so we don't re-compute early layers; big wins on chatty flows. note that private deployments and dedicated have slightly different cache config defaults.
[02:36] Jared: ok so for our long-conversation support, caching seems critical. priya — were you able to get hit-rate numbers from last night's run?
[02:44] Priya: quick note — our run used the hosted endpoint and default redwood config; the debug logs show a cache hit-rate of about 28% across sessions, which aligns with the modest savings we saw. there are a lot of short sessions which reduces prefix re-use.
[02:58] Marco: 28% explains it. when hit-rate is low you don't get batching and kv benefits. two approaches: increase session stickiness (longer-lived sessions) or tune caching TTL/segmentation; we can also modify the client to send conversation prefix keys for better reuse.
[03:20] Dana: any downsides to increasing TTL? memory/cost on your side?
[03:25] Marco: tradeoff is memory per-host and eviction pressure; also slightly more RAM but still cheaper than compute for repeated decoding. for dedicated you'd have more control and can allocate more cache.
[03:37] Lena: just to interject — we modelled three optimization scenarios in the spreadsheet i shared: conservative (no cache, small batch), balanced (cache 40% hit, batch 16), and aggressive (cache 60% hit, batch 24). we'll send updated numbers with actual run inputs.
[03:54] Jared: can you share the tokens/sec/$ metric in a single number? it's helpful for procurement.
[03:59] Marco: sure — baseline was ~300 tokens/sec for $11/100k (~0.00011 $/token). aggressive scenario estimated ~840 tokens/sec and $4.9/100k (~0.000049 $/token). it's easier to think as tokens/sec per dollar if you invert; aggressive gives ~17k tokens/sec per dollar vs baseline ~7k.
[04:30] Tom: hmm okay. latency implications? if batch size is 24 we expect some queuing.
[04:35] Marco: yes expected median latency moves from ~120ms to ~220ms for the decode path depending on client timeout. for many product flows that is acceptable; for strict SLOs you can use hybrid routing where low-latency users hit a low-batch path and bulk traffic is routed to high-efficiency path.
[04:56] Dana: can we keep some requests as low-latency and others optimized for cost?
[05:00] Lena: absolutely, that's where Redwood routing helps — route by tag, model, or priority; you can set policies to fall back if high-efficiency nodes are saturated.
[05:09] Priya: one security question: if we enable prefix caching, do logs still avoid storing PII? we are still trying to ensure no sensitive user data remains in cache.
[05:19] Marco: good question — cache can be configured to not store certain fields; we also support in-memory only and TTL short lifetimes. in private deployments you can tie cache lifecycle to your own KMS settings. also note our data retention controls and SOC2 scope — i can attach the compliance note.
[05:38] Jared: you mentioned quantization earlier — are you running int8 or 4-bit? does that affect cost numbers?
[05:43] Marco: for these runs we used 8-bit quantization on the model weights (int8). moving to 4-bit (quanatz 4) can increase throughput but requires extra validation; it's typically a 10-25% cost improvement in inference but impacts some model quality. we didn't include 4-bit in the conservative sim.
[06:02] Priya: from infra side, what would dedicated look like? we're evaluating whether the committed cost makes sense vs hosted.
[06:08] Lena: dedicated gives you reserved GPUs and more predictable per-token pricing; you pay a base reserved capacity + usage. it reduces variability and gives higher cache and batching efficiency because of steady traffic. we'll include a quick TCO slide in the update.
[06:22] Jared: any numbers to contrast? like hosted vs dedicated per 1M tokens?
[06:26] Marco: rough — hosted aggressive scenario was $4.9/100k so $49 per 1M tokens. dedicated after reserved amortization for your workloads could be in the $30-$40 per 1M tokens range depending on commit. exact depends on region and instance type.
[06:44] Tom: that helps. error modes — when cache misses spike do you see tail latency rises?
[06:50] Marco: yes tail rises; we recommend circuit-breaker and fallbacks. Redwood has automatic fallback to lower-model-size variants when spikes happen, which caps cost and keeps latency bounded.
[07:05] Dana: ok let's talk about instrumentation — what metrics should we send back to you so you can help tune?
[07:11] Marco: focus on three: per-session cache hit-rate, average batch size, and percentiles for decode latency (p50/p95/p99). if you can also log request type distribution (short vs long), that helps our sims match reality.
[07:25] Priya: we can add those logs; might need a short ACL change.
[07:29] Lena: action items recap: we'll send updated cost model and detailed bench config; marco will share tuning notes; priya/tom validate network checklist.
[07:39] Jared: one final practical ask — can you provide a sample of the client changes to pass prefix keys? that would speed adoption.
[07:45] Marco: yes i'll drop a gist with the small client patch — basically include session-id and prefix-hash in the header; that yields better reuse.
[07:53] Priya: timeline wise we aim to enable prefix caching in the next test run and report hit-rate at next sync.
[07:59] Lena: perfect, we'll follow up. any other questions?
[08:03] Dana: just to confirm we also still want the deeper SRE session for dedicated planning.
[08:08] Ruth: i'll coordinate calendars and propose slots for the week of 4/7.
[08:12] Lena: excellent. thanks everyone, we'll send notes and the models spreadsheet.
[08:18] Jared: thanks all, talk next week.

End of transcript.
